o: Concatenate the base-16 representation of n² with the base-36 representation of n³, both uppercase. Example: n = 13 → hex(169)="A9", b36(2197)="1P1" → "A91P1"; n = 36 → "510"+"1000"="5101000". With n ≤ 1000, n³ ≤ 10⁹ — everything fits in standard integer types, so this is a pure base-conversion exercise.
k: One reusable to-base routine with digit alphabet "0123456789ABCDEF…Z" truncated to the base handles both conversions.
Repeated divmod builds digits least-significant first; reverse at the end.

a.i: Write a single converter for any base up to 36 using the shared digit alphabet, call it for (n², 16) and (n³, 36), and concatenate.
s: convert(v, b): repeatedly take v % b, prepend the digit, divide v by b.
a.t: O(log n) — a handful of divisions per conversion.
a.sp: O(log n) for the digit strings.

a.i: Reuse the language's built-in hexadecimal formatter for n² and hand-roll only the base-36 conversion, slightly less code in practice.
s: Format n² with built-in hex helpers (uppercase, no prefix).
Convert n³ to base 36 with divmod and the 36-character alphabet.
a.t: O(log n) — same asymptotics, marginally less code.

w: Trivial problem — the generic converter (Approach 1) is safest across languages since built-in radix support varies. Watch zero handling (n = 1 gives 1 and 1) and uppercase output. Follow-up: generalize to arbitrary bases or signed inputs.
